claims.text: A US court found Google’s general search and text advertising businesses to be monopolies because of its “default-distribution” deals, which the judge ruled were exclusionary conduct.

Specifically:

- Judge Amit Mehta (US District Court for the District of Columbia) issued his liability ruling on 2024‑08‑05, holding that Google violated Section 2 of the Sherman Act by paying companies like Apple, Samsung, and Mozilla billions of dollars to make it their default search engine [Source: ev-1].

witness.reason: claim figures absent from the evidence — untraced: 2

claims.text: - The theory was a self-reinforcing loop: defaults create scale → scale creates data → data improves quality → better quality protects the default position, making it hard for rivals to compete [Source: ev-1].

- Trial evidence showed Google paid roughly $26.3 billion in distribution costs in 2021 (per CEO Sundar Pichai’s testimony) and gave Apple about 36% of Safari search-ad revenue as part of these arrangements [Source: ev-1].

Remedies ordered on 2025‑08‑05 included structural and conduct-based measures:

- Google must divest Chrome — described as the first forced breakup/divestiture of a major tech company since the Microsoft case around 2000 [Source: ev-1].

- Google may no longer pay for default search placement; i.e., it is barred from entering into new revenue-sharing/default-distribution agreements that secure preferred positioning in browsers or devices [Source: ev-1].

claims.text: - The order also imposed limits on certain acquisitions and AI-related investments to prevent re-concentration or entrenchment through those channels [Source: ev-1].
Google appealed to the DC Circuit (notice filed in 2025), arguing the remedies punish procompetitive innovation, so the final outcome remained pending as of late 2025 [Source: ev-1].
